CountingAlgebraNumber Theory
Game: This shows what you get when you add up pairs of numbers in a collection, and asks when two different collections can give exactly the same list of sums.
How to play: Tap the right half of a blue number to make it bigger, or the left half to make it smaller; the arrow keys work too. Change how many numbers there are and how many go into each sum, then press "Show all sums" for the whole list.

    Look for the math
    

      
Take a handful of numbers and add them two at a time. Two completely different handfuls can produce the very same list of answers — but only if the handful has a special size. That is the surprising fact behind this page.


      
Adding numbers two at a time

      
For a multiset A = {a₁, ..., aₙ}, the applet's A₂ is the list of all aᵢ + aⱼ with i < j. For example {2, 3, 6, 9} and {1, 4, 7, 8} both give {5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15}. The "Economize" box is on to begin with: it writes each choice of positions once, ignoring the order you picked them in. Turn it off and every order is listed, so each pair turns up twice.


      
Why the two collections must be the same size

      
A collection of k numbers has C(k, 2) = k(k−1)/2 different pairs of positions, and that count grows as k grows. Two lists that are exactly the same must have the same number of entries, so A and B must have the same size n. The logic test checks that the pair count is strictly increasing, and searches every collection of sizes 1 through 9 made from the numbers 0 to 8: a collision appears only at n = 1, 2, 4, 8.


      
Where the power of two comes from

      
Write the collection as a generating function f(x) = Σ xaᵢ, and do the same for B to get g(x). Squaring counts the sums of two members, so A₂ = B₂ gives f(x)² − g(x)² = f(x²) − g(x²). Factoring and setting h(x) = f(x) − g(x) leaves (f(x) + g(x))h(x) = h(x²). If h is not zero, write it as (1 − x)kp(x) with p(1) ≠ 0; substituting x = 1 gives 2n p(1) = 2k p(1), hence n = 2k−1. That is exactly the page's theorem: a power of two. The logic test confirms the worked example and builds further pairs by the page's own doubling trick.


      
What happens with three or more numbers

      
Using s numbers in each sum gives [f(x)]s − [g(x)]s = f(xs) − g(xs), and the same substitution yields ns−1 = sk−1. The page wonders whether A₃ = B₃ is possible for n = 3 or n = 9, and floats the guess that equal lists force A = B when n is a power of s. The exhaustive test answers both: for s = 3, n = 3, the different collections {0, 3, 3} and {1, 1, 4} both give {3, 3, 6, 6, 6, 9, 9}. So that guess is false — the formula gives a necessary size, not equality. The page itself warns that the general derivation proves less than it seems to; the test agrees.


      
Try the collection {2, 3, 6, 9} with two summonds, then set "How many numbers" to 3 and "How many go into each sum" to 3 and hunt for a second collection with the same list.
